# Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.TaskPool

> `TaskPoolScheduler`, the simplest ready-made `IScheduler`: every item is queued to the .NET thread pool through `Task.Run` the moment it is scheduled. No queue of its own, no ordering, no concurrency limit beyond the pool's, no lifecycle to start or stop, and therefore never an `ExecutionDeclinedException`. `Schedule` blocks the caller until the pool has run the item; `ScheduleAsync` returns a task that completes when it has. One public class, derived from `Scheduler` in `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.Core`. Targets netstandard2.0, netstandard2.1, and net8.0; lives in the `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers` namespace.

Install with `dotnet add package Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.TaskPool`. The type lives in the `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers` namespace - not `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.TaskPool`. One type:

- `TaskPoolScheduler : Scheduler` - public parameterless constructor, not sealed; all 56 `IScheduler` members inherited; `protected override void Enqueue(IScheduled scheduled)` calls `Task.Run(() => scheduled.ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken.None))`

Items run on thread-pool threads, never on the caller's, in no particular order and with no concurrency limit of its own. There is no `Start`, `Stop`, `State`, or `Dispose`; the class implements neither `IService` nor `IDisposable`. A cancellable delegate receives the caller's own `CancellationToken`; a non-cancellable one cannot be interrupted once dispatched. Exceptions reach the caller unwrapped. `Schedule*` capture the caller's `ExecutionContext`; `Unsafe*` run under the default, empty context. For FIFO order, bounded concurrency, or pausing use `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.Channel` instead.
